questions.question: What are the ACID properties of a database transaction?
questions.title: ACID Properties of Database Transactions
questions.direct_answer: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — the four properties that guarantee database transactions are processed reliably. Atomicity ensures all-or-nothing execution, Consistency maintains database rules, Isolation prevents concurrent transaction interference, and Durability guarantees committed data survives system failures.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand what each ACID property means in practice and can explain why each matters with concrete examples.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorizing the four-letter acronym without understanding scenarios where each property prevents data corruption or loss.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the bank transfer example to illustrate all four properties simultaneously, showing how removing any one property breaks data integrity.

sections.title: What ACID Properties Guarantee in Database Transactions
sections.content: ACID properties are the foundation of reliable database transactions. **Atomicity** means a transaction executes completely or not at all — no partial updates. **Consistency** ensures the database moves from one valid state to another, respecting all constraints and rules. **Isolation** prevents concurrent transactions from interfering with each other, so each transaction sees a consistent view of the data. **Durability** guarantees that once a transaction commits, the changes survive system crashes or power failures. Think of ACID like a bank transfer: atomicity ensures both debit and credit happen or neither does, consistency ensures account balances never go negative if that rule exists, isolation prevents two transfers from reading the same balance simultaneously, and durability means your deposited money survives even if the server crashes one second later.

sections.title: ACID at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Atomicity|~All or nothing|every step or none|rollback on failure|debit and credit together
blue|Consistency|~Valid to valid state|constraints enforced|no rule broken|balance never negative
emerald|Isolation|~Concurrent safety|transactions don't interfere|isolation levels|no dirty reads
violet|Durability|~Survives crashes|committed equals permanent|write-ahead log|power-failure safe

sections.title: Spring Transaction with ACID Properties in Action
When You Need ACID Transaction Guarantees
sections.content: Use transactions with ACID guarantees when **multiple database operations must succeed or fail together**. Bank transfers between accounts require atomicity so money isn't lost or duplicated. E-commerce order placement needs consistency to prevent selling more inventory than exists. Multi-user applications need isolation so concurrent updates don't overwrite each other. Financial records need durability so committed transactions survive hardware failures. Any operation where partial completion corrupts your data requires ACID properties.

sections.title: Common Mistakes Freshers Make with ACID
sections.content:
- **Thinking ACID is automatic for all database operations**: Without explicit transaction boundaries in Spring, each repository call is a separate transaction, so multi-step operations aren't atomic.
- **Not understanding isolation trade-offs**: Freshers often don't realize that higher isolation levels prevent more anomalies but reduce concurrency and performance.
- **Ignoring durability assumptions**: Thinking committed data is safe without database backups — durability protects against crashes but not disk failures or accidental deletes.

sections.title: Key Points About ACID Properties
content: **Atomicity**: All operations in a transaction succeed or all fail — no partial updates leave data inconsistent
**Consistency**: Database moves from one valid state to another, all constraints and rules are enforced
**Isolation**: Concurrent transactions don't interfere — each sees a consistent snapshot of data
**Durability**: Committed changes survive crashes, power failures, and system restarts
**Spring enforcement**: at-Transactional annotation ensures ACID properties are applied to service methods
**Trade-offs**: Higher isolation levels provide stronger consistency but reduce performance and concurrency
**Real-world necessity**: Financial operations, inventory management, and multi-step workflows all depend on ACID

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability — four properties that make database transactions reliable. Let me explain each with a bank transfer example. Atomicity means all-or-nothing execution. If you're transferring money between accounts, either both the debit and credit happen or neither does. You can't have money disappear because the debit succeeded but the credit failed. Consistency means the database enforces its rules. If there's a constraint that account balances can't go negative, the transaction won't commit if it would violate that rule. Isolation prevents concurrent transactions from interfering with each other. If two people transfer money from the same account simultaneously, isolation ensures they each see a consistent view and don't corrupt the balance. Durability guarantees that once a transaction commits, the changes survive system crashes. Your deposited money is safe even if the server loses power one second later. In Spring Boot applications, the at-Transactional annotation enforces these properties automatically. Without ACID, multi-step operations would leave your data in inconsistent states — money could vanish, inventory counts could be wrong, and user registrations could be half-completed. That's why ACID is fundamental to reliable database applications, especially in scenarios like financial transactions, order processing, or any workflow where partial completion would corrupt your data.

questions.question: How does Spring's @Transactional annotation work?
questions.title: How @Transactional Works in Spring
questions.direct_answer: The at-Transactional annotation tells Spring to wrap a method in a database transaction, automatically starting the transaction before the method executes and committing on success or rolling back if an unchecked exception is thrown. Spring uses AOP proxies to intercept method calls and inject transaction management code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring knowledge — at-Transactional is used in almost every Spring Data application, so you must understand its behavior.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking at-Transactional works when called from within the same class — Spring's AOP proxy doesn't intercept self-invocation, so the transaction never starts.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the self-invocation caveat and explain that at-Transactional on private methods also doesn't work — only public methods on Spring beans are proxied.

sections.title: How Spring's @Transactional Annotation Manages Database Transactions
sections.content:
Spring's **at-Transactional annotation** uses AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) to automatically wrap methods in database transactions. When you call a transactional method, Spring's **proxy** intercepts the call, starts a database transaction before entering the method, and commits the transaction if the method completes successfully. If an **unchecked exception** (RuntimeException or Error) is thrown, Spring automatically rolls back the transaction. This declarative approach eliminates boilerplate try-catch-commit-rollback code.

Think of it like a bodyguard: the proxy stands between the caller and your method, handling all the transaction lifecycle events (begin, commit, rollback) so your business logic stays clean.

The key is understanding that this only works through Spring proxies — calling a transactional method from within the same class bypasses the proxy entirely.

sections.title: How @Transactional Works
sections.content:
amber|Proxy|~Spring AOP wraps the bean|intercepts the method call|opens a transaction|commits or rolls back
blue|Rollback|~On RuntimeException by default|checked exceptions do NOT roll back|use rollbackFor to change|common trap
emerald|Self-invocation|~Internal call bypasses proxy|this.method() = no transaction|call via injected bean|or use AspectJ
violet|Scope|~Use on the service layer|not the controller|keep the unit of work clear|one transaction per use case

sections.title: Using @Transactional in a Spring Service
When to Apply @Transactional Annotation
sections.content:
Use **at-Transactional on service layer methods** that perform multiple database operations that must succeed or fail together.

Apply it when you're coordinating changes across multiple entities or repositories — order creation with inventory updates, user registration with profile setup, payment processing with status updates.

Use **readOnly = true** for query methods to optimize performance. Don't use at-Transactional on repository methods (they're already transactional) or on methods that don't touch the database. Place it on public methods of Spring-managed beans — private methods and self-invoked methods won't be proxied.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with @Transactional
sections.content:
- **Self-invocation doesn't work**: Calling a transactional method from another method in the same class bypasses the Spring proxy, so no transaction starts. If methodA calls methodB and both have at-Transactional, methodB's annotation is ignored.
- **Using it on private methods**: Spring AOP only proxies public methods, so at-Transactional on private or protected methods is silently ignored.
- **Forgetting checked exceptions roll back differently**: By default, only unchecked exceptions trigger rollback — checked exceptions commit unless you specify rollbackFor.

sections.title: Key Points About @Transactional
content: **Proxy-based**: Spring creates a proxy around your bean that intercepts method calls to manage transactions
**Automatic lifecycle**: Transaction starts on method entry, commits on success, rolls back on unchecked exceptions
**Self-invocation caveat**: Calling transactional methods from within the same class bypasses the proxy
**Public methods only**: Private, protected, or package-private methods aren't proxied, so at-Transactional has no effect
**readOnly optimization**: Mark query methods with readOnly equals true for better performance
**Propagation control**: Nested transactional calls participate in existing transactions by default (REQUIRED propagation)
**Exception handling**: Unchecked exceptions roll back automatically, checked exceptions don't unless configured

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The at-Transactional annotation tells Spring to wrap a method in a database transaction automatically. Spring uses AOP proxies to intercept calls to transactional methods. When you call the method, the proxy starts a transaction before entering your code, and when the method returns successfully, the proxy commits the transaction. If an unchecked exception like RuntimeException is thrown, Spring automatically rolls back the transaction. This declarative approach is much cleaner than writing manual transaction management code. Here's the critical caveat freshers often miss: at-Transactional only works when the method is called from outside the class. If you call a transactional method from another method in the same class, Spring's proxy isn't involved, so no transaction starts. That's called self-invocation and it's a common source of bugs. Also, the annotation only works on public methods of Spring beans — private methods aren't proxied. In a real application, you'd put at-Transactional on service layer methods that coordinate multiple repository calls, like creating an order and updating inventory. That ensures both operations succeed or both fail together. You can also use readOnly equals true on query methods to optimize performance. Understanding how the proxy mechanism works is key to using at-Transactional correctly and avoiding subtle transaction bugs.

questions.question: In practice, when do you actually need a database transaction?
questions.title: When Do You Need a Database Transaction?
questions.direct_answer: You need a database transaction whenever two or more operations must succeed or fail together to maintain data consistency. Any multi-step operation where a partial update would leave your data in an inconsistent state requires a transaction. Single operations that don't depend on other operations typically don't need explicit transactions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment — knowing when to use transactions versus when a single operation doesn't need explicit transaction management.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping every single database call in at-Transactional even when there's only one operation — unnecessary overhead and code clutter.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name specific real-world scenarios: order creation with inventory updates, money transfers, user registration with email verification records — and explain why each requires a transaction.

sections.title: Deciding When Database Transactions Are Necessary
sections.content:
A database **transaction** is necessary when multiple operations must execute as an atomic unit — all succeed or all fail together. The decision hinges on one question: would partial completion leave your data in an **inconsistent state**? If updating table A without updating table B breaks a business rule or corrupts data integrity, you need a transaction. Single operations like saving one entity or running one query typically don't need explicit transactions because each database statement is already atomic. However, coordinating changes across multiple tables, entities, or repositories requires wrapping operations in a transaction.

Think of it like a recipe: if you're making a single dish that doesn't depend on anything else, you don't need coordination. But if you're preparing a multi-course meal where each course must be ready simultaneously, you need orchestration — that's when transactions matter.

sections.title: When You Actually Need a Transaction
sections.content:
amber|Multiple writes, one unit|~Two+ tables must agree|order + inventory + payment|all or nothing|the classic case
blue|Money / inventory|~Correctness is critical|no partial debit|no oversell|always wrap
emerald|Read-modify-write|~Avoid lost updates|read balance, then update|concurrent users|needs isolation
violet|Not needed|~Single-row insert/update|one atomic statement|already atomic|don't over-wrap

sections.title: Wrapping a Multi-Step Operation
Step 1: Identify Multi-Step Operations Requiring Atomicity
sections.content: Start by asking: does this operation involve multiple writes that depend on each other? **Order creation** typically requires inserting an order record, updating inventory quantities, and creating order line items — all three must succeed or the system is inconsistent. **Money transfers** require debiting one account and crediting another — you can't have money disappear or duplicate. **User registration** might involve creating a user record, saving a profile, and inserting an email verification token — partial completion leaves orphaned data. If the answer is yes, you need a transaction. Single writes like saving one user or fetching one order don't need explicit transactions.

sections.title: Step 2: Evaluate the Cost of Inconsistency
sections.content: Ask: what happens if this operation partially succeeds? If the consequence is **data corruption**, **financial loss**, or **broken business rules**, use a transaction. For example, charging a customer's credit card but not creating their order is a critical failure requiring a transaction. If the consequence is minor and recoverable — like a cache miss or a delayed log entry — a transaction might be overkill. Also consider **concurrency**: if two users updating the same data simultaneously could cause conflicts, you need transaction isolation. Real-time inventory updates under heavy traffic require transactions to prevent overselling.

sections.title: Common Mistakes Deciding When to Use Transactions
sections.content:
- **Over-transacting**: Wrapping every repository method in at-Transactional even when there's only one database operation — this adds unnecessary overhead and makes code harder to read. Spring Data repositories are already transactional for single operations.
- **Under-transacting**: Not using transactions for multi-step workflows like order processing, leading to inconsistent data when one step fails.
- **Ignoring read-only scenarios**: Not marking read-only methods with readOnly equals true, missing performance optimizations for queries that don't modify data.

sections.title: Key Points About When to Use Transactions
content: **Multi-step coordination**: Use transactions when two or more operations must succeed or fail together to maintain consistency
**Single operations don't need them**: One repository save or one query doesn't require explicit at-Transactional — already atomic
**Financial operations**: Money transfers, payments, refunds always need transactions to prevent loss or duplication
**Inventory management**: Stock updates coordinated with order creation require transactions to prevent overselling
**User workflows**: Registration, profile setup, permission assignment — multi-table changes need transactions
**Concurrency protection**: High-traffic scenarios where simultaneous updates could conflict need transaction isolation
**Read-only optimization**: Mark query methods with readOnly equals true for better performance, even if single operation

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: You need a database transaction whenever multiple operations must succeed or fail together to keep your data consistent. The key question is: would partial completion break something? Let me give you concrete examples. Order creation almost always needs a transaction. You're inserting an order record, updating inventory quantities, and creating order line items. If the order saves but the inventory update fails, you've oversold your stock. That's inconsistent, so you wrap it in at-Transactional. Money transfers definitely need transactions. Debiting one account and crediting another must happen atomically — you can't have money vanish or duplicate. User registration is another common case. You're creating a user record, saving their profile, and maybe inserting an email verification token. If the user saves but the profile creation fails, you have orphaned data. On the flip side, single operations usually don't need explicit transactions. If you're just saving one entity or running one query, Spring Data repositories handle that atomically already. Wrapping every single repository call in at-Transactional is a common mistake freshers make — it adds overhead and clutter without benefit. Here's a practical rule: if you're calling multiple repository methods and all those changes must be visible together or not at all, use a transaction. If you're doing one thing that doesn't depend on anything else, skip it. Also think about concurrency. High-traffic inventory systems need transactions to prevent race conditions where two requests try to buy the last item simultaneously. In summary, use transactions for multi-step operations where consistency matters, like financial workflows, order processing, and user registration flows.

questions.question: What are the four database transaction isolation levels and what read anomalies do they prevent?
questions.title: Transaction Isolation Levels Explained
questions.direct_answer: The four isolation levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE. Each prevents progressively more read anomalies: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Higher isolation means better consistency but lower concurrency and performance.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the trade-off between consistency and performance in concurrent database access and can explain what anomalies each level prevents.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking SERIALIZABLE is always best — it prevents all anomalies but serializes concurrent transactions, severely hurting throughput.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Know that MySQL's default is REPEATABLE READ and PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED — and be able to say which anomalies each prevents with examples.

sections.title: Understanding Database Isolation Levels and Read Anomalies
sections.content:
Transaction **isolation levels** define how much one transaction can see changes made by other concurrent transactions. The four standard levels — **READ UNCOMMITTED**, **READ COMMITTED**, **REPEATABLE READ**, and **SERIALIZABLE** — form a spectrum from weakest to strongest isolation.

Each level prevents specific **read anomalies**: dirty reads (reading uncommitted changes), non-repeatable reads (reading different values in the same transaction), and phantom reads (seeing new rows appear mid-transaction). Higher isolation provides stronger consistency guarantees but reduces concurrency because transactions must wait for locks. Lower isolation allows more concurrent access but risks anomalies. Most databases default to READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL, Oracle) or REPEATABLE READ (MySQL) as a practical balance between consistency and performance.

sections.title: Isolation Levels and Anomalies
sections.content:
amber|READ UNCOMMITTED|~Lowest|allows dirty reads|sees uncommitted data|rarely used
blue|READ COMMITTED|~Postgres default|stops dirty reads|non-repeatable reads possible|solid default
emerald|REPEATABLE READ|~MySQL default|stops non-repeatable reads|phantoms still possible|stronger
violet|SERIALIZABLE|~Highest|stops phantom reads too|acts fully serial|slowest, most locking

sections.title: Choosing an Isolation Level
Step 1: Understand the Three Read Anomalies
sections.content: **Dirty reads** happen when you read uncommitted data from another transaction that might roll back — your data is based on changes that never actually happened. **Non-repeatable reads** occur when you read the same row twice in your transaction and get different values because another transaction modified and committed it in between. **Phantom reads** are when you run the same query twice and see different rows because another transaction inserted or deleted rows matching your criteria. Understanding these anomalies is the foundation for choosing isolation levels — each level prevents a different subset of these problems.

sections.title: Step 2: Match Isolation Level to Anomaly Prevention Needs
sections.content: **READ UNCOMMITTED** prevents nothing — allows all three anomalies but offers maximum concurrency. **READ COMMITTED** prevents dirty reads only — you see only committed data but repeated reads can return different values. **REPEATABLE READ** prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads — the same row always returns the same value within your transaction. **SERIALIZABLE** prevents all three anomalies — transactions execute as if they ran one after another sequentially. Choose based on your consistency requirements: report generation might tolerate non-repeatable reads for speed, while financial calculations might need REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE to ensure accurate totals.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Isolation Levels
sections.content:
- **Defaulting to SERIALIZABLE for everything**: Freshers think the highest isolation is always safest, but SERIALIZABLE can severely hurt performance by forcing transactions to wait, causing timeouts and deadlocks in high-concurrency scenarios.
- **Not knowing database defaults**: MySQL defaults to REPEATABLE READ while PostgreSQL defaults to READ COMMITTED — assuming one behavior across databases leads to bugs.
- **Ignoring the performance cost**: Higher isolation levels require more locking, which reduces throughput and can cause contention bottlenecks under load.

sections.title: Key Points About Isolation Levels
content: **READ UNCOMMITTED**: No isolation, allows all anomalies, rarely used in practice due to dirty read risks
**READ COMMITTED**: Prevents dirty reads, default for PostgreSQL and Oracle, good balance for most applications
**REPEATABLE READ**: Prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads, default for MySQL, ensures consistent row values
**SERIALIZABLE**: Prevents all anomalies, strongest consistency, but lowest concurrency and performance
**Trade-off principle**: Higher isolation equals better consistency but worse performance and concurrency
**Database differences**: MySQL and PostgreSQL have different defaults and implement levels differently
**Spring configuration**: Set isolation in at-Transactional with isolation equals Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The four isolation levels are READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ, and SERIALIZABLE. They control what changes from other concurrent transactions you can see. Each level prevents specific read anomalies. Let me explain the three anomalies first. A dirty read is when you read uncommitted data that might get rolled back — you're seeing changes that never actually happened. A non-repeatable read is when you read the same row twice and get different values because another transaction modified it in between. A phantom read is when you run the same query twice and see different rows because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows. Now here's what each level prevents. READ UNCOMMITTED prevents nothing — it's rarely used because dirty reads are too risky. READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable and phantom reads. This is PostgreSQL's default and works well for most applications. REPEATABLE READ prevents dirty and non-repeatable reads, ensuring the same row always returns the same value within your transaction. MySQL uses this as its default. SERIALIZABLE prevents all three anomalies by making transactions execute as if they ran one after another sequentially. Here's the key trade-off freshers miss: higher isolation gives better consistency but hurts performance and concurrency. SERIALIZABLE is the safest but can cause major bottlenecks because transactions have to wait for locks. In practice, READ COMMITTED is usually good enough unless you're doing financial calculations where you need consistent totals across multiple reads. Then you'd use REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE. Always know your database's default — MySQL's REPEATABLE READ is stricter than PostgreSQL's READ COMMITTED, which can cause confusion if you switch databases.

items: You see duplicate entries or wrong counts under load — you may need a higher isolation level or a unique constraint
Throughput drops and you see lock wait timeouts — you may be at SERIALIZABLE when REPEATABLE READ would suffice

speakable_v2.cap: Know the four levels, their anomalies, and the defaults — then only increase isolation if you've confirmed an anomaly problem.

questions.question: What is transaction propagation in Spring and what is the difference between REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW?
questions.title: Spring Transaction Propagation: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
questions.direct_answer: Transaction propagation defines how a transactional method behaves when called from within another transaction. REQUIRED, the default, joins the existing transaction if one is active or starts a new one if not. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely independent new transaction.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of transaction propagation — shows you know that at-Transactional has behavior beyond just wrapping a method in begin/commit/rollback.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that REQUIRED is the default, or thinking every at-Transactional always creates a new transaction regardless of context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a use case for REQUIRES_NEW: audit logging that should be committed even if the main transaction rolls back, or processing individual batch items independently.

sections.title: How Transaction Propagation Controls Nested Transaction Behavior
sections.content:
**Transaction propagation** determines what happens when a transactional method calls another transactional method. Spring supports seven propagation types, but **REQUIRED** and **REQUIRES_NEW** are the most common. **REQUIRED** (the default) means the method participates in the existing transaction if one is active, or starts a new one if not — this creates seamless transaction boundaries across method calls. **REQUIRES_NEW** always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely independent new transaction — changes in the inner transaction commit or roll back independently of the outer transaction.

Think of REQUIRED like carpooling: if someone's already driving (a transaction exists), you join that ride. REQUIRES_NEW is like taking your own car: you're independent regardless of whether others are traveling.

sections.title: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
sections.content:
amber|REQUIRED|~The default|join the caller's transaction|or start one if none|one shared unit of work

sections.title: REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW
REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW Propagation

rows: Rolls back only its own transaction

sections.title: When to Use Each Propagation Type
sections.content:
Use **REQUIRED** (the default) for normal business logic where all operations should succeed or fail together — order creation calling inventory updates, user registration calling email sending. The entire workflow shares one transaction.

Use **REQUIRES_NEW** when you need an operation to commit independently regardless of the outer transaction's fate. Classic examples: audit logging that must be saved even if the main operation fails, processing batch items where each item's success or failure shouldn't affect others, or recording error details when a transaction is already marked for rollback. REQUIRES_NEW is the exception, not the rule — most service methods should use REQUIRED.

sections.title: Common Mistakes with Transaction Propagation
sections.content:
- **Not knowing REQUIRED is the default**: Freshers think every at-Transactional starts a new transaction, but by default methods join existing transactions, which is usually what you want.
- **Overusing REQUIRES_NEW**: Creating independent transactions everywhere breaks atomicity — if orderService calls inventoryService with REQUIRES_NEW, the inventory update commits even if the order creation fails.
- **Ignoring self-invocation**: Propagation only applies when Spring's proxy intercepts the call — calling a REQUIRES_NEW method from within the same class doesn't create a new transaction.

sections.title: Key Points About Transaction Propagation
content: **REQUIRED default**: Most methods use REQUIRED propagation, joining the existing transaction or creating one if needed
**REQUIRES_NEW independence**: Creates a new transaction and suspends the current one, commits and rolls back independently
**Audit logging pattern**: REQUIRES_NEW is perfect for audit logs that must be saved even if the main transaction fails
**Batch processing use case**: Process individual items in REQUIRES_NEW so one failure doesn't roll back all items
**Rollback scope difference**: REQUIRED shares rollback with outer transaction, REQUIRES_NEW isolates its rollback
**Configuration syntax**: Specify with at-Transactional(propagation equals Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
**Performance consideration**: REQUIRES_NEW has overhead — it suspends and resumes transactions, use it only when truly needed

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Transaction propagation controls what happens when a transactional method calls another transactional method. The two most important types are REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW. REQUIRED is the default propagation. It means if there's already a transaction active, the method joins that transaction. If there's no transaction, it starts a new one. This is what you want most of the time because it creates seamless transaction boundaries. For example, if your orderService creates an order and calls inventoryService to update stock, both operations happen in the same transaction. If either fails, both roll back together. REQUIRES_NEW is different. It always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely independent new transaction. The inner transaction commits or rolls back on its own, regardless of what happens to the outer transaction. Here's a concrete use case: audit logging. Say you want to log every order attempt, even if the order creation fails. You'd mark your audit logging method with REQUIRES_NEW. That way, when the logging method commits, the audit record is saved permanently, even if the outer order transaction rolls back. Another use case is batch processing where you want to process items independently — if item three fails, items one and two should still be committed. The key mistake freshers make is not knowing REQUIRED is the default, or overusing REQUIRES_NEW and breaking atomicity. In most scenarios, you want operations to share a transaction, which is what REQUIRED gives you. Only use REQUIRES_NEW when you genuinely need an operation to commit independently.

groups.heading: REQUIRED (default)
groups.text: If there's already an active transaction, the method joins it. If there's none, a new one starts. All operations share the same unit — if the outer transaction rolls back, the inner one rolls back too.

groups.heading: REQUIRES_NEW
groups.text: Always suspends the current transaction and starts a completely new one. The inner method commits or rolls back independently. Even if the outer transaction later rolls back, the inner one's commit stands.

items: Use REQUIRED (default) when: the inner method is part of the same logical operation — publishing a post and updating the author's count
Use REQUIRES_NEW when: the inner operation must commit even if the outer fails — audit logging a failed post attempt

beats.text: In our blog: when a user publishes a post, we log the audit event. Use REQUIRES_NEW on logAuditEvent() — if the post publish fails and rolls back, the audit record still commits. That way you always have a record of the attempt.

speakable_v2.cap: REQUIRED is right for most cases; REQUIRES_NEW is the exception for operations that must commit regardless of the outer result.
